TENTATIVE RULING(S):

PROCEDURAL/FACTUAL BACKGROUND
This is a post-judgment petition seeking the sale of a parcel of residential rental real property
located at 13788 Gemini Street, Victorville, CA, 92392 (APN 3095-212-12-0000) (“Subject
Property”), by Petitioner/Judgment Creditor Barry A. Ross, APC, against Respondent/Judgment
Debtor Jacques Simon.

On October 21, 2025, the Court entered an Order for Sale of the Property (“Sale Order”),
following consideration on Petitioner’s Motion for Order for Sale of Real Property (“Sale Motion”)
filed on May 9, 2025.

Between February 6, 2026 to March 13, 2026, Respondent filed four (4) separate ex parte
applications, essentially seeking reconsideration of the Sale Order. The Court denied the first
three ex parte applications. However, on March 13, 2026, the Court partially granted the fourth
ex parte application, to the extent of advancing and shortening time to hear the instant Motions
on March 27, 2026. The Court also imposed a temporary stay on the sale of the Subject
Property and set a briefing schedule for the Motions. The Court ordered Respondent Simon to
post bond in the amount of $5,800 as part of the TRO under CCP section 529.
On March 20, 2026, Petitioner filed an Opposition. On March 23, 2026, Respondent filed a
Reply.

DISCUSSION
I. Request for Judicial Notice
In opposition, Petitioner requests the Court take judicial notice of the following documents:
• Exhibit 1 – Judgment filed in Barry Ross, APC v. Jacques Simon, Case No. 30-
2022-01253607-CL-PA-CJC, in the Orange County Superior Court on September
22, 2022 (“OC Action”);
• Exhibit 2 – Writ of Execution issued on March 17, 2025 in the OC Action;
• Exhibit 3 – Memorandum of Points and Authorities in Support of Order for Sale of
Real Property Dwelling filed in this Action on May 9, 2025;
• Exhibit 4 – Proof of Service of Sale Motion filed in this Action on June 18, 2025;
• Exhibit 5 – Minute Order filed in this Action on October 8, 2025;
• Exhibit 6 – Order to Show Cause as to Why an Order for Sale Should Not Issue
Pursuant to C.C.P. Section 704.770(a), filed in this Action on October 8, 2025;
and
• Exhibit 7 – Order for Sale of Real Property filed in this Action on October 21,
2025.

The Court may take judicial notice of “[r]ecords of (1) any court of this state or (2) any court of
record of the United States or of any state of the United States” including its register of actions
(Evid. Code § 452, subd. (d); City and County of San Francisco v. Carraro (1963) 220
Cal.App.2d 509, 527.) While “[a] court may take judicial notice of the existence of each
document in a court file, [it] can only take judicial notice of the truth of facts asserted in
documents such as orders, findings of fact and conclusions of law, and judgments.” (People v.
Thacker (1985) 175 Cal.App.3d 594, 599 (italics in original).)
The Court GRANTS Petitioner’s request to take judicial notice of Exhibits 1 - 7, pursuant to
Evidence Code section 452, subdivision (d).

II. Statement of Law – Reconsideration Motion
Code of Civil Procedure section 1008, subdivision (a), provides for the mechanism by which a
party may seek reconsideration of a court’s earlier order or ruling. In general, a motion for
reconsideration must: (1) be made within 10 days after service of the notice of entry of the order; (2)
be based on new or different facts, circumstances or law; and (3) be accompanied by a
declaration stating what previous “application” was made, the ruling thereon, and what new or
different facts, circumstances or law are claimed to exist. (Code Civ. Proc., § 1008, subd. (a).)
III. Analysis – Reconsideration Motion
At the outset, the two Motions appear to be a disguised motion for reconsideration because
Respondent essentially seeks a revocation of the Sale Order. However, a motion for
reconsideration made pursuant to Code of Civil Procedure section 1008, either filed by parties or
brought sua sponte by the court itself, “is the exclusive means for modifying, amending or
revoking an order” and that limitation is expressly jurisdictional. (Baldwin v. Home Sav. of
America (1997) 59 Cal.App.4th 1192, 1200.) Although the Motions are not expressly brought or
titled as a “motion for reconsideration,” the name of a motion is not controlling, and, regardless
of the name, a motion asking the trial court to decide the same matter previously ruled on is a
motion for reconsideration under Code of Civil Procedure section 1008. (Lennar Homes of
California, Inc. v. Stephens (2014) 232 Cal.App.4th 673, 681; Powell v. County of Orange (2011)
197 Cal.App.4th 1573, 1577.)
Here, there are no new or different facts presented that would justify the lifting of the Sale
Order. Here, the evidence regarding a lack of service on tenants, the death of Petitioner’s former sole
principal, and the subsequent corporate dissolution of Petitioner (Set Aside Mot. at pp. 5-6; Quash
Motion at pp. 5-6), existed and were discoverable well before the hearing on the Sale
Motion on October 8, 2025. A motion for reconsideration may be properly denied where it is
based on evidence that could have been presented in connection with the original motion.
(Hennigan v. White (2011) 199 Cal.App.4th 395, 406.)
The Motions also appears to argue that the Court’s prior ruling on the Sale Motion is erroneous,
specifically on the basis that the Court misapplied the dwelling sale procedures (Code Civ. Proc.
§§ 704.710, 704.710, 704.740) to a non-dwelling rental property. (See Set Aside Mot. at pp. 4-5; Quash
Motion at p. 5.) However, although the issue of the purported misapplication of the law
was not briefed or discussed in the prior Sale Motion, the presentation of “different law” in
support of a motion for reconsideration is also insufficient to warrant reconsideration, absent
satisfactory explanation for the moving party’s failure to present this different law before initial
ruling. (Baldwin v. Home Sav. of America (1997) 59 Cal.App.4th 1192, 1198-1199.) Here,
Respondent provides no adequate explanation as to why the issue of misapplication of the law
was not raised in the Sale Motion.

Respondent states that he suffered physical injuries resulting from a hit-and-run accident and a
work-place injury before the hearing on the Sale Motion. (Simon Decl. ¶¶ 2-5). However,
Respondent’s purported physical injuries did not appear to materially impact Respondent’s ability
to mount an opposition to the Sale Motion. Here, Respondent was able to prepare and file an
opposition to the Sale Motion and was also able to personally appear and make oral arguments
at the hearing on October 8, 2025. If he could not do so, he had the option of locating a
competent attorney to represent him. In fact, Respondent admits that his inability to retain an
attorney was purportedly caused by a decrease in financial resources; and was not instead
caused by his physical injuries. (See Simon Decl. ¶ 9.) Although Respondent states that his
financial situation prevented him from seeking legal advice, Respondent does not state that he
made any efforts to locate and retain low-cost or free legal aid or services and was denied.
Although Respondent was formally representing himself in propria persona, when a litigant
represent himself in propria persona, “he is entitled to the same, but no greater, consideration
than other litigants and attorneys” (Bistawros v. Greenberg (1987) 189 Cal.App.3d 189, 193) and
is not entitled to lenient treatment on that basis (Rappleyea v. Campbell (1994) 8 Cal.4th 975,
979).

Additionally, a party’s motion asking the court to reconsider a ruling on its own motion after the
10-day period is ineffective. (Farmers Ins. Exchange v. Superior Court (2013) 218 Cal.App.4th
96, 102, fn 10.) The court is not obliged to rule on it and opposing counsel need not respond.
(Ibid.) The California Supreme Court concluded that the requirements of section 1008 for
reconsideration of orders are jurisdictional as applied to the parties. (Le Francois v. Goel (2005)
35 Cal.4th 1094, 1104-1105.) Unless the requirements of section 1008 are satisfied, any motion
to reconsider must begin with the court on its own motion. (Ibid.)
Given this, the Court DENIES the Motions on the basis that they were untimely filed when
construed under section 1008 as the motions were filed more than 10 days from the Court
Clerk’s service of the Court’s ruling on the Motion to Stay on October 8, 2024. (Code Civ. Proc.,
§ 1008, subd. (a).)
Although it is not necessary for the Court to address Respondent’s remaining arguments, the
Court elects to provide the following substantive analysis on the Motions based on Code of Civil
Procedure section 473, subdivision (b).

IV. Statement of Law – Set Aside Motion
Under Code of Civil Procedure section 473, subdivision (b), “the court may, upon any terms as
may be just, relieve a party … from a judgment, dismissal, order, or other proceeding taken
against him or her through his or her mistake, inadvertence, surprise, or excusable neglect.” The
application shall be made within a reasonable time, in no case exceeding six months, after the
judgment, dismissal, order, or proceeding was taken. (Code Civ. Proc. § 473, subd. (b).)
The term “proceeding,” as used in section 473, subdivision (b), incorporates “ ‘[a]ll the steps or
measures adopted in the prosecution or defense of an action.’ [Citation.]” (Zellerino v. Brown
(1991) 235 Cal.App.3d 1097, 1105 (Zellerino).) Accordingly, section 473, subdivision (b) may
afford parties relief from the consequences of a wide variety of procedural errors committed in
the course of an action. (Maynard v. Brandon (2005) 36 Cal.4th 364, 372.)
V. Analysis - Set Aside Motion
A. Whether Mistake, Inadvertence, Surprise, or Excusable Neglect is Sufficiently
Demonstrated?

In general, the party moving for relief on the basis of “mistake, inadvertence, surprise, or
excusable neglect” must show specific facts demonstrating that one of these conditions was met.
(Hopkins & Carley v. Gens (2011) 200 Cal.App.4th 1401, 1410 [defendant’s burden to
demonstrate “that due to some mistake, either of fact or of law, of himself or of his counsel, or
through some inadvertence, surprise or neglect which may properly be considered excusable,
the judgment or order from which he seeks relief should be reversed” (emphasis in original;
internal quotes omitted)].)
Relief may be granted on a showing of mistake by a party or attorney. Such mistake may be one
of fact or law, but in either case, it must be material. (Weil & Brown, Cal. Practice Guide: Civil
Procedure Before Trial (The Rutter Group 2026) ¶ 5:311.) An honest mistake of law is a valid
ground for relief where a problem is complex and debatable.” (Brochtrup v. INTEP (1987) 190
Cal.App.3d 323, 329.) The controlling factors in determining whether a mistake was excusable
are (1) the reasonableness of the misconception and (2) the justifiability of the failure to
determine the correct law. (Community Redevelopment Agency v. Superior Court (1967) 248
Cal.App.2d 164, 174.)
“Surprise” requires “some condition or situation in which a party ... is unexpectedly placed to his
injury, without any default or negligence of his own, which ordinary prudence could not have
guarded against.” (Baratti v. Baratti (1952) 109 Cal.App.2d 917, 921.)
Finally, “inadvertence” or “excusable neglect” requires establishing the default could not have
been avoided through the exercise of ordinary care. (Hearn v. Howard (2009) 177 Cal.App.4th
1193, 1206 [holding that “the acts which brought about the default must have been the acts of a
reasonably prudent person under the same circumstances”].)
Here, Respondent argues that reasonable excuse is demonstrated because Respondent was
physically injured in a hit-and-run accident that occurred on July 5, 2024. In connection with that
injury, Respondent was proscribed with pain relievers (ibuprofen) and muscle relaxants
(cyclobenzaprine), which was taken daily to manage Respondent’s pain and spasms.
Respondent also underwent numerous chiropractic sessions and physical therapy sessions.
Thereafter, on January 10, 2025, Respondent was further injured at work and was taken off work
until January of 2026. (Simon Decl. ¶¶ 2-5.)
Respondent testifies that these injuries prevented him from meeting court deadlines, organizing
a proper defense, or preparing a “full” opposition to the Sale Motion and states that he was
“unable to fully explain” his arguments to the Court in a manner that he would have desired.
Respondent also states that he was unable to “fully” participate at the hearing due to his injuries,
which purportedly included “mental repercussions.” Respondent also admits that he was unable
to afford legal representation due to a decrease in financial resources caused by his physical
injuries and a loss of work. (Simon Decl. ¶¶ 6-9.)
Here, as discussed above, Respondent’s purported physical injuries did not appear to materially
impact Respondent’s ability to mount an opposition to the Sale Motion and it does not appear
that Respondent has acted as a reasonably prudent person under the circumstances.
Nevertheless, apart from any statute, courts have the inherent authority to vacate a judgment on
equitable grounds such as extrinsic fraud or extrinsic mistake. (Bae v. T.D. Service Co. of
Arizona (2016) 245 Cal.App.4th 89, 97.) “Extrinsic fraud usually arises when a party is denied a
fair adversary hearing because he has been ‘deliberately kept in ignorance of the action or
proceeding, or in some other way fraudulently prevented from presenting his claim or defense.’”
(Ibid.) The terms “extrinsic fraud or mistake” are given a broad meaning and tend to encompass
almost any set of extrinsic circumstances which deprive a party of a fair adversary hearing. (In re
Marriage of Park (1980) 27 Cal.3d 337, 342 (Marriage of Park).) There need be no actual “fraud”
or “mistake” in the strict sense. (Ibid.)
Accordingly, the Motions will nonetheless be analyzed on the merits for consideration as to
whether there was any extrinsic fraud in reaching the Court’s ruling on the Sale Motion and all
subsequent proceedings undertaken in conjunction with the Sale Order (i.e., the enforcement of
the Writ of Execution and the Sheriff’s Sale Notice), and therefore those proceedings should be
set aside on that basis, or alternatively, whether those proceedings should be stayed under
Code of Civil Procedure section 918.

B. Whether Relief Should be Granted on the Merits?
Respondent argues that the Sale Order and all subsequent proceedings undertaken in
conjunction with the Sale Order should be set aside, or alternatively, stayed, on the following
grounds: (i) the Court misapplied the law in regard to real properties that are not occupied by the
judgment creditor; (ii) there was a lack of service on the tenants residing at the Property; (iii)
Petitioner lacked standing to prosecute the Action due to the untimely death of Petitioner’s
former sole principal, Barry A. Ross, and the subsequent corporate dissolution of Petitioner; and (iv)
because it would be inequitable to force the sale of the Property.
i. Whether the Court Misapplied the Law?

Respondent argues that in reaching a decision on the Sale Motion, the Court erroneously
invoked the sale procedures of Code of Civil Procedures section 704.740, despite the fact that
the Property was not occupied by the Respondent.

In support, Respondent argues that Code of Civil Procedures section 704.710 defines a
“dwelling” as the place where the judgment debtor actually resides. This is incorrect. Code of
Civil Procedure section 704.710, subdivision (a), which provides the definition of a “dwelling,”
states in full:
(a) “Dwelling” means a place where a person resides and may include but is not limited to the
following:
(1) A house together with the outbuildings and the land upon which they are situated.
(2) A mobilehome together with the outbuildings and the land upon which they are situated.
(3) A boat or other waterborne vessel.
(4) A condominium, as defined in Section 783 of the Civil Code.
(5) A planned development, as defined in Section 11003 of the Business and Professions Code.
(6) A stock cooperative, as defined in Section 11003.2 of the Business and Professions Code.
(7) A community apartment project, as defined in Section 11004 of the Business and Professions
Code.
(Code Civ. Proc., § 704.710, subd. (a).)
Furthermore, Code of Civil Procedure section 704.740, subdivision (a), states that with the
exception of subdivision (b), which is inapplicable here, “the interest of a natural person in a
dwelling may not be sold under this division to enforce a money judgment except pursuant to a
court order for sale obtained under this article and the dwelling exemption shall be determined
under this article. (Emphasis added.) Accordingly, neither the statutory definition of a “dwelling”
nor the application of Code of Civil Procedure section 704.740 is limited to places where a
judgment debtor may reside.

Moreover, Code of Civil Procedure section 704.740 simply imposes the additional requirement of
a court order for sale of a dwelling in order to determine whether the homestead exemption
applies. (Wells Fargo Financial Leasing, Inc. v. D & M Cabinets (2009) 177 Cal.App.4th 59, 72
[“The statute thus clearly and unambiguously makes a section 704.740 order a requirement for
sale of a dwelling subject to a homestead exemption…”]; see also Gonzalez v. Toews (2003)
111 Cal.App.4th 977, 984 [holding that “the only purpose for the section 704.740 court order
proceeding is to determine the homestead or “dwelling exemption.”].) In general, a court order is
not required if the property is not a “dwelling.” (Weil & Brown, Cal. Practice Guide: Enforcing
Judgments and Debts (The Rutter Group 2025) ¶ 6:760.)
Additionally, Respondent’s misapplication of the law argument is not an “extrinsic” mistake
warranting setting aside of the Sale Order.

In general, equitable relief is available only where the fraud or mistake was “extrinsic”—meaning
the party was denied the opportunity to be heard. (In re Marriage of Melton (1994) 28
Cal.App.4th 931, 937.) When a claim of fraud goes to an issue involving the merits of the prior
proceeding which the moving party should have guarded against at that time, or if the moving
party was guilty of negligence in failing to prevent the fraud or mistake or in contributing thereto,
or failed to take advantage of liberal discovery policies to fully investigate their claim, any fraud is
intrinsic fraud. (In re Marriage of Stevenot (1984) 154 Cal.App.3d 1051, 1069.) “Fraud is intrinsic
and not a valid ground for setting aside a judgment when the party has … had an opportunity
to present his case and to protect himself from any mistake or fraud of his adversary, but has
unreasonably neglected to do so.” (Ibid.)
Here, Respondent was not prevented from participating in the Sale Motion proceedings and was
able to file an opposition and attend the hearing. Accordingly, no extrinsic fraud is demonstrated.
ii. Whether there was a Lack of Service on Tenants?
Respondent argues that Petitioner failed to serve a copy of the Notice of Sale and the Sale
Motion on the tenants of the Property pursuant to Code of Civil Procedure sections 701.545 and
704.770, subdivision (b).

However, Petitioner presents evidence that the Sheriff mailed a copy of the Notice of Sale to
Respondent on January 28, 2026 and also personally served a copy of Notice of Sale to an
individual by the name of “Dana Hays” at the Property on February 2, 2026 at 11:27 a.m.
(Froelich Decl. ¶ 17, Exh. 7.)
In regard to the Sale Motion, Petitioner presents evidence of the proof of service filed on June
18, 2025, which demonstrates that a copy of the Sale Motion and all related documents were
mailed both to Respondent at his Long Beach residence, and also a separate copy was mailed
to the Property. (RJN Exh. 4.)
On reply, Respondent argues, without providing any legal authority, that all tenants must be
served. However, a point merely suggested with no supporting argument or authority is deemed
to be without foundation and requires no discussion. (See Do It Urself Moving v. Brown, Leifer,
Slatkin & Berns (1992) 7 Cal. App. 4th 27, 35, superseded by statute on other grounds Union
Bank v. Sup.Ct. (1995) 31 Cal. App. 4th 573, 582-583).)
Furthermore, the issue regarding a purported lack of service on the tenants, alone, is insufficient
to demonstrate that there was extrinsic fraud imposed on the Respondent, himself. As discussed
above, Respondent was not prevented from participating in the Sale Motion proceedings and
was able to file an opposition and attend the hearing. To the extent that it is argued that improper
service was effectuated on the tenants of the Property, it is incumbent on those parties to seek
appropriate relief from the Court on their own behalf, especially because it is sufficiently
demonstrated that tenants have at least received mail service of the Motion and personal service
of the Notice of Sale.
iii. Whether Petitioner Lacked Standing?

Respondent also argues that Petitioner lacked standing to prosecute the Action due to the
untimely death of Petitioner’s former sole principal, Barry A. Ross, in July 28, 2024 and the
subsequent corporate dissolution of Petitioner on June 25, 2025.
In opposition, Petitioner argues that the Judgment is an asset of Barry Ross’ Estate, as it was
entered before his untimely death on September 22, 2022. (RJN Exh. 1.) After his death in July
2024, the shares of the corporation went into the Barry A. Ross and Myra C. Ross Family Trust
dated April 3, 1991 (“Ross Estate”), which is managed by Michelle Ross, the successor trustee.
(Ross Decl. ¶¶ 4-6, Exh. 8.) Although Petitioner underwent a corporate dissolution on June 25,
2025, Ms. Ross is currently still winding up the assets and directed the filing and prosecution of
the Sale Motion. (Ross Decl. ¶¶ 7-8.)
Corporations Code section 1903, subdivision (b), states that when a voluntary proceeding for
winding up a corporation has commenced, the board shall continue to act as a board and shall
have full powers to wind up and settle its affairs, both before and after the filing of the certificate
of dissolution. Furthermore, under Corporations Code section 2010, subdivision (a), “[a]
corporation which is dissolved nevertheless continues to exist for the purpose of winding up its
affairs, prosecuting and defending actions by or against it and enabling it to collect and
discharge obligations, dispose of and convey its property and collect and divide its assets, but
not for the purpose of continuing business except so far as necessary for the winding up
thereof.”
Thus, corporate control over the Petitioner may continue to operate despite its dissolution for the
purpose of winding up its affairs. As such, Respondent’s lack of standing argument is not
sufficiently demonstrated.

On reply, Petitioner argues that Petitioner was required to disclose the death of Barry Ross in
this Action and to make an appropriate substitution under Code of Civil Procedure section
377.31, et seq. However, under Code of Civil Procedure section 377.31, a substitution of a
successor in interest or personal representative applies following the “death of a person.” In
contrast, here, Petitioner is a corporate entity, and as discussed above, it nevertheless continues
to exist for the purpose of winding up its affairs despite the filing of a certificate of dissolution.
iv. Whether Equity Justifies a Stay or Set Aside Order?
Respondent argues that setting aside or staying the execution of the sale of the Property is
nonetheless justified because Respondent opines that the Property is worth in excess of
$400,000.00 and would be inequitable to force a sale of the Property over a debt of $23,274.23.
However, any hardship or inequitable result on Respondent is not sufficiently demonstrated if
enforcement of the Judgment is not permitted. As acknowledged by Respondent, given the
valuation of the Property, any sale of the Property is likely to generate funds in excess of the
amount owed to Petitioner, which will be paid to Respondent. Further, the Property is
undisputedly an investment rental property, thus, Respondent will not face the consequences of
being displaced from his home.

Therefore, the Court DENIES Respondent’s Motion to Stay Order for Sale of Real Property and
Motion to Set Aside/Vacate Order for Sale of Real Property.

RULING
Based on the foregoing analysis, the Court rules as follows:
(1) GRANTS Petitioner’s request to take judicial notice of Exhibits 1 - 7, pursuant to
Evidence Code section 452, subdivision (d)
(2) DENIES Respondent’s Motion to Stay Order for Sale of Real Property and Motion to
Set Aside/Vacate Order for Sale of Real Property, with prejudice.
(3) LIFTS temporary stay on sale of the Subject Property, and the sale of the Subject
Property shall proceed without further delay.
